---
title: "CLT Convergence for Exponential Samples"
format: html
editor: visual
---

### 

## Background

The exponential distribution has its most common value at 0 with bigger values getting progressively less common, but with all results still greater than or equal to 0. Because its shape is so distinct from a normal curve, it is likely to take a long time for the sample means to converge.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(6418)

# 2. Simulation parameters
B <- 10000                            # Number of Monte Carlo repetitions
n_values <- c(2, 5, 10, 30, 100)         # Sample sizes to test

# 3. Initialize results data frame
results <- data.frame()

# 4. Run Monte Carlo loop
for (n in n_values) {
  
  # Draw B sample means from Exponential(rate = 1)
  sample_means <- replicate(B, mean(rexp(n, rate = 1)))
  
  # A. Calculate Q-Q Plot R-squared
  theo_quantiles <- qnorm(ppoints(B))
  sample_quantiles <- sort(sample_means)
  r2_val <- cor(theo_quantiles, sample_quantiles)^2
  
  # B. Calculate Sample Skewness (3rd standardized moment)
  m3 <- mean((sample_means - mean(sample_means))^3)
  s3 <- sd(sample_means)^3
  skew_val <- m3 / s3
  
  # C. Calculate Excess Kurtosis (4th standardized moment - 3)
  m4 <- mean((sample_means - mean(sample_means))^4)
  s4 <- sd(sample_means)^4
  kurt_val <- (m4 / s4) - 3
  
  # Append to results
  results <- rbind(results, data.frame( 
    n = n,
    R2 = r2_val,
    Skewness = skew_val,
    Excess_Kurtosis = kurt_val
  ))
}

# ==============================================================================
# Generate Plots with 3xSE Threshold Overlays
# ==============================================================================

# Graph 1: Q-Q Plot R^2 vs. Sample Size (Threshold = 0.98)
p1 <- ggplot(results, aes(x = n, y = R2)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.98, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = max(n_values), y = 0.98, label = "Normality Threshold (0.98)", 
           vjust = -0.5, hjust = 1, color = "firebrick", fontface = "bold") +
  labs(
    title = expression(bold("1. Quantile Alignment (" * R^2 * " vs. Sample Size)")),
    subtitle = expression("Exponential Parent (" * B == 10000 * ")"),
    x = "Sample Size (n)",
    y = expression("Q-Q Plot " * R^2)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = n_values) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Graph 2: Skewness vs. Sample Size (Threshold = 0.075)
p2 <- ggplot(results, aes(x = n, y = Skewness)) +
  geom_line(color = "darkorange", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "darkorange", size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.075, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = min(n_values), y = 0.075, label = "Normality Threshold (0.075)", 
           vjust = -0.5, hjust = 0, color = "firebrick", fontface = "bold") +
  labs(
    title = "2. Asymmetry (Skewness vs. Sample Size)",
    subtitle = expression("Exponential Parent (" * B == 10000 * ")"),
    x = "Sample Size (n)",
    y = "Skewness"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = n_values) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Graph 3: Excess Kurtosis vs. Sample Size (Threshold = 0.15)
p3 <- ggplot(results, aes(x = n, y = Excess_Kurtosis)) +
  geom_line(color = "forestgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "forestgreen", size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.15, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = min(n_values), y = 0.15, label = "Normality Threshold (0.15)", 
           vjust = -0.5, hjust = 0, color = "firebrick", fontface = "bold") +
  labs(
    title = "3. Tail Weight (Excess Kurtosis vs. Sample Size)",
    subtitle = expression("Exponential Parent (" * B == 10000 * ")"),
    x = "Sample Size (n)",
    y = "Excess Kurtosis"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = n_values) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Display plots
print(p1)
print(p2)
print(p3)
```

While R\^2 and kurtosis pass their tests relatively quickly, skewness doesn't even come close at n=100. This requires further investigation of the behavior at high values of n.

```{r}
# ==============================================================================
# Refinement Simulation: Exponential Parent (Skewness Crossover - Coarse Search)
# ==============================================================================

library(ggplot2)

# 1. Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(6418)

# 2. Simulation parameters
B <- 10000                            # Number of Monte Carlo repetitions
n_values <- seq(100, 1000, by = 100)  # Multiples of 100 between 100 and 1000

# 3. Initialize storage
results <- data.frame()
sim_data <- list()                    # List to store raw sample means vectors

# 4. Run Monte Carlo loop for Exponential(rate = 1)
for (n in n_values) {
  
  # Draw B sample means from Exponential(rate = 1)
  sample_means <- replicate(B, mean(rexp(n, rate = 1)))
  
  # Save raw sample means to sim_data for potential visual checks
  sim_data[[as.character(n)]] <- sample_means
  
  # Calculate Sample Absolute Skewness (3rd standardized moment)
  m3 <- mean((sample_means - mean(sample_means))^3)
  s3 <- sd(sample_means)^3
  skew_val <- abs(m3 / s3)
  
  # Append to results data frame
  results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
    n = n,
    Skewness = skew_val
  ))
}

# Print numerical summary table to console
print(results)

# ==============================================================================
# Generate Skewness Plot with 0.075 Threshold Overlay
# ==============================================================================

p_skewness_zoom <- ggplot(results, aes(x = n, y = Skewness)) +
  geom_line(color = "darkorange", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "darkorange", size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.075, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = max(n_values), y = 0.075, label = "Threshold (0.075)", 
           vjust = -0.5, hjust = 1, color = "firebrick", fontface = "bold") +
  labs(
    title = "Asymmetry (|Skewness| vs. Sample Size)",
    subtitle = "Exponential Parent — Coarse Search",
    x = "Sample Size (n)",
    y = "|Skewness|"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = n_values) +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

This graph, unfortunately, is not very useful. At these values of n, the change in the skewness of the samples is significantly smaller than the standard error of the skewness, causing the graph to jump around and hide any trend that may exist. It is possible to calculate the exact value of n directly, although this requires forknowledge that the skewness of n is exactly $\frac{2}{\sqrt{n}}$. Solving for n when this eqation equals 0.075 yields n=712.

```{r}
# ==============================================================================
# Visual Validation Plots for Exponential Parent at n = 1000
# ==============================================================================

# Extract raw n = 1000 sample means from sim_data list
df_n1000 <- data.frame(sample_means = sim_data[["1000"]])

# Graph v1: Histogram + Density (Unimodality Check)
v1 <- ggplot(df_n1000, aes(x = sample_means)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)), 
    bins = 50, 
    fill = "steelblue", 
    color = "white", 
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_density(color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = expression(bold("Visual Check for Unimodality")),
    subtitle = "Sample Means at n = 1000",
    x = "Sample Mean",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Graph v2: Normal Q-Q Plot for n = 1000
v2 <- ggplot(df_n1000, aes(sample = sample_means)) +
  stat_qq(color = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5, size = 1) +
  stat_qq_line(color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = expression(bold("Normal Q-Q Plot")),
    subtitle = "Sample Means at n = 1000",
    x = "Theoretical Quantiles",
    y = "Sample Quantiles"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Display visual validation plots
print(v1)
print(v2)
```

Even the visual check shows lingering non-normal artifacts at n=1000.

## Conclusion

As expected, the distribution took a long time to converge to normal. The convergence definitely happens above n=100, but the exact value is impossible to calculate due to limitations of monte carlo simulations. This does not mean it does not converge, it just means that monte carlo simulations are a fundamentally flawed way to calculate these values.

## $$\boxed{n=\text{Uncalculable}}$$
